# Introduction

{{< include ../include/activate_environment.qmd >}}

Welcome to this interactive Julia tutorial which introduces the basics of variables and types. Understanding variables and their types is crucial as they are the building blocks of any program. They determine how data is stored, manipulated, and how efficiently your code runs.

This script is designed to be interactive. Follow the instructions, write your code in the designated code blocks, and then execute the corresponding code. Each exercise is followed by an `@assert` statement that checks your solution.

## Julia in Zed

1. First, install the **Julia** extension for syntax support: open the command palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`, macOS `Cmd+Shift+P`), choose **zed: extensions**, and search for "Julia".
2. Create (or pick) the folder where you want to save all the files for this course.
3. Open a terminal in that folder and run:
   ```
   julia --project=.
   ```
   The `.` means 'this folder': Julia uses your course folder as the environment.
4. In the Julia REPL that opens, run:
   ```julia
   using Pkg
   Pkg.add("IJulia")  # Add IJulia to the environment
   ```
5. Still in Julia, run:
   ```julia
   using IJulia
   zed_plots = raw"""
   push!(Base.package_callbacks, pkg -> pkg.name == "Plots" &&
       @eval Base.showable(::MIME"text/html", ::$(Base.loaded_modules[pkg]).Plot) = false)
   """
   IJulia.installkernel("Applied Optimization", "--project=" * abspath("."), "-e", zed_plots)
   write(".JETLSConfig.toml", """
   [[diagnostic.patterns]]
   pattern = "(lowering|inference)/undef-global-var"
   match_by = "code"
   match_type = "regex"
   severity = "off"
   path = "**/tutorial-*.jl"
   """)
   ```
   This creates a Jupyter kernel that uses the course environment: it is how Zed runs Julia code. The `zed_plots` part makes your plots visible in Zed: Zed cannot show the web version of a plot yet, so the kernel sends plots as images instead. The `write` line saves a settings file for Zed's Julia extension in your course folder. Without it, the extension underlines the test cells of every tutorial with "… is not defined", because they check variables that you only create when you solve the exercise.
6. Type `exit()` or press Ctrl+D to exit the Julia REPL. If Zed was open during these steps, quit it completely (macOS: `Cmd+Q`) and start it again: Zed only reads its kernels when it starts.
7. Download this tutorial as a `.jl` file from the course website and save it in your course folder. You can do so by clicking on the "Julia" link in the sidebar (under "Code Links") on the tutorial page. Keep all tutorial files there, together with the `data` folders some of them need later: Zed's Julia extension then knows the course packages.
8. In Zed, open your course folder and open the `.jl` file from there: the settings file from step 5 only works while the course folder is open. The file is split into cells by `# %%` markers.
9. Put the cursor in a cell and press `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` (also on macOS), or run **repl: run** from the command palette. This runs the cell and jumps to the next one. Output appears right below the code. Zed picks the kernel by itself: the kernel selector at the top right of the editor should show the kernel that starts with **applied-optimization** — that is the kernel you just installed. If it shows another one (such as `julia-1.13`), click it and choose yours.

:::{.callout-warning}
Sorry that the start is rather complicated. But by following these steps, you get a clean environment to work in and you basically cannot break anything by installing packages.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
These steps ensure you're working in a clean Julia environment for the course. The `--project=.` flag tells Julia to use your course folder itself as the environment: the course packages live there, in the files `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`, and stay separate from your other projects. The kernel remembers the exact Julia version it was installed with: close Zed before you update Julia (for example with `juliaup update`), then run steps 3 and 5 again.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Fallback: VS Code
If Zed does not run on your machine (for example, an older Windows GPU without DirectX 11), install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com) with the [Julia](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=julialang.language-julia) extension instead. Open the same `.jl` file there: the extension recognizes the `# %%` cell markers, and `Alt+Enter` (or `Shift+Enter`) runs the current cell in the Julia REPL using the course environment.
:::

# Section 1 - Variables

Think of variables as labeled containers. Just like you might label a box "Books" to store books, in programming we label our data with variable names. For example:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
age = 30        # A box labeled "age" containing the number 30
```
```{julia}
#| eval: true
name = "Tobias"  # A box labeled "name" containing the text "Tobias"
```

Declare a variable named `x` and assign it the value `1`.

```{julia}

# Test your answer
@assert x == 1 "Check again, the value of x should be 1. Remember to assign the value directly to x."
println("Great, you have correctly assigned the value $x to the variable 'x'.")
```

Always replace 'YOUR CODE BELOW' with your actual code.

# Section 2 - Basic Types

Just like real containers come in different types (like boxes for books, refrigerators for food, etc.), variables in Julia have different types depending on what they store:

- Integers (Int): Whole numbers like `1`, `42`, `-10`
- Floats (Float64): Numbers with decimal points like `3.14`, `-0.5`
- Booleans (Bool): True/false values like `true`, `false`
- Strings (String): Text in quotes like `"Hello"`

You can check what type of "container" a variable is using `typeof()`. Try this:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
age = 25
typeof(age)     # Will show Int64 (integer type)
```
```{julia}
#| eval: true
price = 19.99
typeof(price)   # Will show Float64 (decimal number type)
```

# Section 3 - Type Annotations and Inference

Sometimes we want to specify exactly what kind of "container" we want to use. In Julia, we can do this using type annotations. Why should you care? Later in the course, JuMP will insist on the right kinds of numbers for your optimization models, and telling Julia the exact type also helps it run your code fast.

```{julia}
#| eval: true
temperature::Float64 = 37.0    # Specifically saying we want a decimal number
```
```{julia}
#| eval: true
n_items::Int64 = 100           # Specifically saying we want a whole number
```

## Exercise 3.1 - Type Annotation

Declare a variable `y` with an explicit type annotation of `Int64` and assign it the value `5`.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# YOUR CODE BELOW

```
```{julia}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
# Test your answer
@assert y == 5 && typeof(y) == Int64 "Make sure 'y' is of type Int64 and has the value 5."
println("Great! You've created an Int64 variable 'y' with the value $y.")
```

# Section 4 - String Interpolation

String interpolation is like filling in blanks in a sentence. Instead of writing:
```{julia}
#| eval: true
name = "Tobias"
age = 30
# The hard way:
message = "My name is " * name * " and I am " * string(age) * " years old"
```

We can use the `$` symbol to insert variables directly into our text:
```{julia}
#| eval: true
message = "My name is $name and I am $age years old"
```

It's like having a template where Julia automatically fills in the values for you! If you have paid attention to the previous exercise, you have already seen this in action. The following example illustrates this again:

```{julia}
#| eval: true
language = "Julia"
println("I'm learning $language")
```

## Exercise 4.1 - String Interpolation

Create a string `message` that says `"y is [value of y]"` using string interpolation. This uses the variable `y` you created in Exercise 3.1 - if you get an `UndefVarError`, run that exercise again first.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# YOUR CODE BELOW

```
```{julia}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
# Test your answer
@assert message == "y is 5" "Make sure your string includes the correct value of y."
println("Excellent! Your interpolated string is: $message")
```
